title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
statement: You are given an array of strings, each exactly four characters long and of the form a==b or a!=b, where a and b are single lowercase letters standing for variables. Return true if integers can be assigned to the variables so that every equation holds at once, and false otherwise.
realWorld: Constraint solving in a type checker: unification collects a stream of "these two type variables are the same" facts, and a later "these two must differ" fact has to be checked against everything unified so far. Record deduplication has the same shape - a pile of "these rows are the same customer" merges plus a few "these two are definitely different people" rules that must not be violated.

examples.explanation: The first makes a and b the same value; the second demands they differ. No assignment satisfies both.
Both say the same thing. Assigning a = b = 1 works, so redundant equalities never cause a contradiction.

The two equalities put a, b and c in one group, which contradicts c!=a. Note the order: at the moment c!=a is read, a and c are still unrelated, and only the equations that come afterwards create the conflict.

bruteForce.whySlow: Each inequality re-walks the equality graph from scratch and re-derives the very same partition of the letters that the previous inequality just derived. The traversal computes a complete grouping and then throws all of it away to return one bit. The grouping never changes after the equalities are read, so with 500 equations this is up to 500 full traversals of a structure that has been fixed since the first pass.

patternIdentification: Two kinds of statement are in play: one that merges things (== is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it defines an equivalence relation) and one that only reads the merge (!= asserts nothing new, it just forbids). Whenever a problem mixes "these are the same" with "these must differ", build all of the sameness first with union-find, then evaluate every difference against the finished partition. The order is not a stylistic choice: it is why the two kinds cannot be interleaved, because an equality read later can join two letters that an inequality checked and accepted earlier, and nothing goes back to re-check it.

optimized.idea: Two passes over the same array. Pass one ignores every != and unions the two letters of every ==, which leaves each connected group of letters sharing one root - the partition is now final, whatever order the equalities appeared in. Pass two ignores every == and, for each !=, fails the moment find(a) equals find(b). Only 26 slots are ever needed, and a!=a is caught for free, since a letter is always its own root. Doing this in a single pass is the classic bug, and example 3 is the input that exposes it: c!=a is satisfiable when it is read and unsatisfiable by the time the array ends.

commonMistakes: Checking each != as it is read, in one pass over the array - [c!=a, b==a, b==c] returns true, because when c!=a was tested a and c were still in separate groups and nothing ever revisits that decision.

Parsing only characters 0 and 3 and unioning on every equation - [a==b, b!=c] then merges b with c and immediately reports false, rejecting a system that is perfectly satisfiable with a = b = 1 and c = 2.

Reading the operator from index 2 instead of index 1 - index 2 is always =, so every equation is treated as an equality, and a self-contradiction like [a!=a] becomes the harmless union(a, a) and returns true.
